title: Greedy Algorithms
description: Learn how Greedy Algorithms make locally optimal decisions, why they are efficient, and when greedy reasoning succeeds or fails.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Greedy Algorithms solve problems by repeatedly making the best possible choice at the current moment.

Instead of exploring every possible solution, a greedy algorithm immediately selects what appears to be the most beneficial, efficient, or optimal local decision.

After making a choice, the algorithm moves forward without reconsidering previous decisions. This often creates fast and memory-efficient solutions.

sections.title: Why Greedy Algorithms Matter
sections.content:
Many real-world systems require fast decision making. Scheduling systems, shortest path algorithms, and optimization systems often cannot afford to test every possible solution.

Greedy Algorithms reduce computational cost by immediately committing to locally optimal decisions instead of performing exhaustive search.
bullets: Many optimization systems rely on greedy reasoning.

sections.title: Core Idea of Greedy Algorithms
sections.content:
A Greedy Algorithm repeatedly evaluates available choices, selects the locally best option, permanently commits to that choice, and continues until the solution is complete.

Unlike Dynamic Programming, greedy methods usually do not revisit decisions, backtrack, or explore every possibility.

sections.title: Local vs Global Optimization
sections.content:
A locally optimal choice means choosing the best immediate option. A globally optimal solution means achieving the best final overall result.

The challenge is that local decisions do not always guarantee the globally best solution. Some problems allow greedy reasoning to work correctly, while others do not.

sections.title: Greedy Choice Property
sections.content:
A problem can often be solved greedily if it satisfies the Greedy Choice Property.

This means making locally optimal choices still leads toward a globally optimal solution.

Problems such as Activity Selection, Huffman Coding, and Dijkstra’s Algorithm satisfy this property.

sections.title: Optimal Substructure
sections.content:
Optimal Substructure means the optimal solution can be built from optimal solutions to smaller subproblems.

Many greedy algorithms rely on both the Greedy Choice Property and Optimal Substructure.

sections.title: Coin Change Example
sections.content:
Suppose we need to make 18 pesos using coins 10, 5, and 1.

A greedy strategy repeatedly selects the largest possible coin.

The algorithm selects 10, then 5, then three 1-peso coins. This quickly reduces the remaining amount and minimizes unnecessary smaller denominations.

sections.title: Why Greedy Algorithms Are Fast
sections.content:
Greedy Algorithms avoid exhaustive search, backtracking, and testing every combination.

Instead, they immediately commit to decisions. This often produces lower time complexity, lower memory usage, and faster execution.

chart.title: Greedy algorithm efficiency
chart.description: Greedy Algorithms often avoid exhaustive exploration, producing more scalable performance than brute-force search.

sections.title: When Greedy Algorithms Fail
sections.content:
Greedy Algorithms do not always produce optimal solutions.

Suppose the coin values are 1, 3, and 4, and the target amount is 6.

A greedy strategy selects 4 first, then two 1s, producing 3 coins total. However, the optimal solution is 3 + 3, which uses only 2 coins.

This demonstrates that local optimal choices can sometimes produce globally suboptimal solutions.

sections.title: Greedy Algorithms vs Dynamic Programming
sections.content:
Greedy Algorithms prioritize efficiency and simplicity by making immediate decisions.

Dynamic Programming explores many subproblems and revisits decisions to guarantee optimal solutions.

Greedy methods are usually faster and more memory efficient, while Dynamic Programming often provides stronger correctness guarantees.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content: Greedy implementations commonly involve sorting, repeated selection, and immediate commitment to locally optimal choices.

codeSnippets.title: Simple greedy coin selection
codeSnippets.code:
coins = [10, 5, 1]
amount = 18
selected = []

for coin in coins:
    while amount >= coin:
        selected.append(coin)
        amount -= coin

print(selected)

codeSnippets.title: Largest-first selection example
codeSnippets.code:
numbers = [3, 8, 2, 9, 5]
selected = []

while numbers:
    largest = max(numbers)
    selected.append(largest)
    numbers.remove(largest)

print(selected)

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Greedy Algorithms appear in GPS route calculation, network routing, CPU scheduling, compression systems, cloud infrastructure, and optimization systems.

Modern systems frequently rely on fast local decision making to process large workloads efficiently.

subsections.title: Misconception: Greedy Algorithms always find the best solution
subsections.content: Greedy reasoning only works correctly for certain problem structures.

subsections.title: Misconception: Greedy Algorithms are random shortcuts
subsections.content: Greedy decisions follow carefully designed optimization logic.

subsections.title: Misconception: Fast algorithms are always greedy
subsections.content: Many efficient algorithms use recursion, graph traversal, or Dynamic Programming instead.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Greedy Algorithms make locally optimal decisions.
Greedy methods usually do not revisit earlier choices.
Some problems satisfy the Greedy Choice Property.
Greedy Algorithms are fast and memory efficient.
Greedy reasoning does not always guarantee optimal solutions.
Understanding when greedy works is an important algorithmic skill.
